etymology_text: Unknown. Henry Ludwig Fr. Lutz opted to read the sign 𒄯 with the common value ḫar instead of mur, requiring one occurrence containing mu-ur- as referring to another plant, and deems the remainder to render Arabic *أَخُو أَرْضٍ (*ʔaḵū ʔarḍin, literally “earth brother”). This seems out of question since we realize that the modern value [dˤ], now transcribed superficially similarly ḍ, was in antiquity a voiced alveolar lateral fricative [ɮˤ]. Neither afford مَرْد (mard, “toothbrush-tree fruits”) thorns, as behoves by the Akkadian descriptions, or Arabic in general any transferrable ending. The structure hints to an Anatolian loanword with a privative a.

etymology_text: Usually regarded as a loanword from some other non-Semitic or Afroasiatic language. Has been compared to Middle Egyptian pꜣ-ꜣb(w) (with the Egyptian definite article prefixed; reconstructed as /piʀ-ˈʀuːbaw/), from which Ancient Greek ἐλ-έφας (el-éphas) (whence also English elephant) and Latin eb-ur (“ivory”) are borrowed, too. Blažek 1998 postulates Proto-Semitic *pirl-, with assimilation r-l → r-r or r-l → l-l, yielding Akkadian forms 𒉿𒄿𒊒 (pīru) and 𒉿𒄿𒇻 (pīlu). Has also been compared with Proto-Berber *eḷu, and speculated to have been borrowed via Egyptian to account for the initial p- (as the prefixed definite article), though no such word seems to be attested in Egyptian.

head_templates.expansion: libittum f (construct state libitti, plural libnātum)

etymology_text: From a reconstructed Proto-Semitic *labin(a)t (“brick”); diffusing to other Semitic languages via the Akkadian term seems difficult to account and there has been no compelling reason to assume the Akkadian is the original source. More distantly a possible connection to Proto-Semitic *laban- (“dairy”) with compared developed verbal senses, to strain milk or yogurt of its whey, to thicken or coagulate, to solidify, to dry out, to become firm or solid pieces; hence the connection to drying and solidifying of bricks. Compare Eblaite 𒇷𒁀𒌈 (li-ba-tum /⁠libittum, libattum⁠/), Ugaritic 𐎍𐎁𐎐𐎚 (lbnt, “brick”), Hebrew לְבֵנָה (ləḇenɔ́, “sun-baked or dried-out brick”), Aramaic לְבִינְּתָּא (/⁠ləḇinṯā, ləḇittā⁠/), Classical Syriac ܠܒܬܐ (/⁠ləḇettā⁠/), Arabic لِبْنَة (libna) and لَبِنَة (labina).

etymology_text: Compare Aramaic מְנָא (mənā, “to count, to number”), Aramaic מַנְיָא (manyā, “mina”), Arabic مَنًى (manan, “fate, lot, destiny”) and Arabic مُنِيَة (muniya, “desire”) and Biblical Hebrew מָנָה (mānâ, “to count, to number”)

etymology_templates.name: cog
etymology_templates.expansion: Biblical Hebrew מָנָה (mānâ, “to count, to number”)

glosses: to count, reckon, list (individual objects, animals, persons, units of time)

categories.name: Akkadian entries with incorrect language header

glosses: to wait (for a number of days)

examples.text:
𒅎𒉡𒋳𒈠𒀸𒀀𒎌𒌑𒉺𒅁𒅆𒄴
[imnūšum-ma ina mê ušap[šiḫ]]
im-nu-šum-ma AŠ A-MEŠ ú-šap-š[i-iḫ]
He recited it and bro[ught ca]lm into the waters.
examples.ref: Enūma Eliš, line 63

glosses: to hand over, deliver (objects or persons to someone)
to charge (interest, deliveries, etc. to someone), reckon (against someone)
to consider (a person, a region, an object as belonging to a specific class, region, or destination)
to assign, deliver (persons or objects) (with ana/ina: to the responsibility of someone)
to change, turn into (with ana or -iš: used with terms for destruction, annihilation, etc.)

examples.english: You put ingots which were not good before my messenger and said: "If you want to take them, take them; if you do not want to take them, go away!"

head_templates.expansion: nakrum (feminine nakirtum or nakartum, masculine plural nakrūtum, feminine plural nakrātum, predicative nakir)

etymology_text: From [script needed] (nakārum, “to be hostile”).

examples.english: I have sent as messengers gentlemen like ourselves to collect the bag with my money (deposited with you) but you have treated me with contempt by sending them back to me empty-handed several times, and that through enemy territory.
examples.translation: I have sent as messengers gentlemen like ourselves to collect the bag with my money (deposited with you) but you have treated me with contempt by sending them back to me empty-handed several times, and that through enemy territory.
